Every organisation has its data spread over multiple systems, sometimes even in vast data lakes. For example, support agents log tickets, sales teams update the CRM, engineers file bugs in the bug tracker, and most of the conversational context ends up in Slack threads and emails. Each tool is good at its own job, so over time what the organisation knows, and more importantly what it needs to make business-critical decisions, is spread across all of them.

Let's visualise the need for a central organisational knowledge search using a few synthetic examples. Say a product manager at a bike company wants to know why customers are asking for refunds . The answer is already somewhere in the data. For example, a support ticket might have details about a brake cable that snapped, an email could mention a battery that dies after 10 km, and a Slack message might include conversational details about three customers wanting their money back over faulty brakes. But this data is spread across three tools, written by three different people, and not in the same words.

The obvious first step is to search for "refund". The search will most probably return the refund policy, the refund how-to and the email, all of which include the word "refund". It will most certainly miss the ticket and the Slack message, which describe the problem in different words. The manager gets an answer that looks complete but isn't.

The problem isn't that the data is missing or incomplete. The problem is that search looks for word matches, and people often describe the same thing using different words. For an organisation to make business-critical decisions based on data it already has, search has to work across every source and understand what a query means instead of just looking for word matches.

Data is connected from many sources. Indexing runs when there's new data. Retrieval runs when a user searches.

This post walks through three types of retrieval using the same dataset of ten notes, shows where each approach fails and builds up to what a good retrieval strategy looks like:

- Text search , the approach behind most search boxes

- Embedding search , the approach that matches the semantic meaning of natural-language queries

- Embedding search with a reranker , similar to embedding search but with a second layer of intelligence that reranks results for relevance

For each method we'll look at how the data goes through two paths of the search system:

- Indexing is the write path. It runs when a document is created or changed, and prepares it for lookup.

- Retrieval is the read path. It runs on each query, looks for matching documents and returns the result.

## 1. Text search: match exact words

Text search matches the exact words in the query to the index. It's what Postgres full-text search, Elasticsearch and Lucene do underneath, and it powers most search boxes on the internet.

Indexing. A connector posts each document to the search API. The API then runs the text through an analyzer , which splits it into tokens, converts them to lowercase, drops stop words like "the" and "so", and does some lexical processing. Each processed term is inserted into an inverted index , which is a map from the indexed word to a posting list including the ids of every document that contains it. For example, adding note 10 to the inverted index would append 10 to the posting lists for terms "money", "back", "brake" and the rest.

Retrieval. The query goes through the same analyzer that's used for indexing, so "Brakes" and "brake" become the same term. The API fetches the posting list for each term, merges them and ranks the documents. This demo ranks by how many query terms a document matches. Production engines use more sophisticated ranking functions such as BM25 , which weights rare terms above common ones and adjusts for document length.

Try "refund", "money back" and "equipment failures".

Word matches are not enough: Text search is fast and easy to debug, but a document matches only when it contains the exact word. This is a good retrieval system for IDs, product codes, error messages and names but falls short for data with paraphrased natural language. In our example, refund returns notes 1, 3 and 9: the policy, the battery complaint and the how-to. Money back means the same thing but returns only note 10. Note 2, the snapped brake cable, won't show up in either search. And equipment failures doesn't match anything, even though all three notes describe exactly that using different words . Synonym lists can help match individual cases, but then you end up maintaining a thesaurus for every way people describe a problem, and you'll still miss paraphrases and have to deal with false positives from loose synonyms.

## 2. Embedding search: match the meaning

Embedding search keeps both paths and the same API. However, it swaps two components where the analyzer becomes an embedding model and the inverted index becomes a vector database .

Indexing. The API sends each document's text to the embedding model, which returns a vector : a fixed-length array of floats. We use bge-small-en-v1.5 in this example, which returns 384 of them.
